Online customer support means helping customers in writing, through a screen, instead of across a counter. The customer cannot see your smile or hear your voice. Everything they feel about the business comes from **how fast you reply, what your words say, and whether you do what you promised**. In this course you will learn to do that well, on the channels Nigerian customers really use, and to keep simple records that show your work.

A support request is any message where a customer needs something: a question before buying ("Do you deliver to Ibadan?"), a problem after buying ("My order has not arrived"), a change ("Please change the size to 42") or a complaint ("The cream you sent is leaking"). Your job is to understand the request, solve it or pass it to the right person, and tell the customer clearly what happens next.

Online support is written support: your reply speed and wording are the whole customer experience.

Matching the request to the channel

A simple rule: **keep quick things quick, and move serious things to a record**. A customer who asks the price of a bag on WhatsApp should get the answer on WhatsApp. A customer who wants a refund of ₦45,000 should still get a fast, warm reply on WhatsApp, but the refund details (order number, amount, bank details for the refund, date promised) should be confirmed in writing in a way the business can find again, for example by email or in your tracking sheet.
**Pre-sale question** (price, size, delivery area): answer on the same channel, quickly.
**Order status** ("Where is my order?"): check the record first, then reply with a specific date or step.
**Problem or complaint**: acknowledge fast, collect details, log it, give a time for the next update.
**Money matters** (refunds, double payment): confirm details in writing and follow the business's approval rule. Never promise money you are not allowed to approve.
Worked example: one morning's messages
For example, Ngozi supports a small skincare brand in Enugu. At 9:00 am she opens WhatsApp Business and finds 6 unread chats and 1 email.

She scans all 7 first instead of answering the top one. 3 are price questions, 1 is "Where is my order?", 1 is a customer saying a jar arrived cracked, 1 is a wholesale enquiry, and the email is a refund request.
She answers the 3 price questions in about 5 minutes using saved replies (you will build these in Lesson 1.2).
For the order question she checks her sheet, sees the parcel left on Monday with the dispatch rider, and replies with the expected delivery day.
For the cracked jar she replies at once: she apologises, asks for a photo and the order number, and promises an update by 2:00 pm.
She forwards the wholesale enquiry to the owner with a one-line summary, and tells the customer the owner will reply today.
She acknowledges the refund email, logs it, and asks the owner for approval.
All 7 customers had a first reply within 30 minutes. The two serious cases were logged with a promised update time, so nothing was forgotten.

Your three promises

Customers judge support on three things. **Speed**: a quick first reply, even if it only says you are checking. **Clarity**: short sentences, specific facts, a clear next step. **Follow-through**: if you say "I will update you by 2 pm", you update them by 2 pm, even if the news is "still waiting". Breaking a promise does more damage than a slow first reply.

Writing your automatic messages
Automatic messages should be short, warm and honest. Never promise an instant answer if you cannot give one.

**Greeting:** "Hello, welcome to Ada's Kitchen 👋. Thank you for your message. Please tell us your name and what you need, and we will reply within 30 minutes during opening hours (Mon to Sat, 8 am to 6 pm)."
**Away:** "Thank you for your message. We are closed now and will reply from 8 am tomorrow. For orders, please send the item name, quantity and delivery area so we can help you faster."

Support agents see a lot of private information: names, phone numbers, home addresses, payment receipts, sometimes ID or medical details. In Nigeria, the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023** sets rules for how organisations collect and use personal data, and it is overseen by the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)**. You do not need to be a lawyer, but you must follow the basic principles: collect only what you need, use it only for the reason you collected it, keep it secure, and do not share it without a proper reason.
A person protecting private data on a screen
Customer data belongs to the customer; you are only looking after it.
Everyday privacy rules for agents
Ask only for what you need. To deliver an order you need a name, phone number and address. You do not need a date of birth.
Never post a customer's chat, receipt or address in a group or on a status, even as a joke or "lesson". If you use a real chat in your portfolio, remove names, numbers and addresses.
Do not discuss one customer's order with another person unless the customer has said that person can collect or ask.
Lock your phone and laptop. Log out of shared computers.
Delete or archive old files you no longer need, following the business's rule.

Worked example: spotting a fake alert

For example, Bisi handles orders for a phone accessories shop in Abuja. A new customer orders 4 power banks at ₦18,000 each and sends a screenshot showing a ₦72,000 transfer. He asks for urgent dispatch because he is "travelling in one hour".
Bisi checks the order total: 4 × ₦18,000 = ₦72,000. The amount matches.
She replies: "Thank you, Emeka. We will dispatch as soon as the payment reflects in our business account. I am confirming now."
She asks the owner to check the business bank app. After 20 minutes, no money has arrived.
She replies politely: "We have not received the transfer yet. Please check with your bank. We will dispatch once it reflects."
The customer becomes aggressive and then stops replying. Bisi labels the chat and notes it in the tracking sheet.
No goods were lost. The urgency, the screenshot and the pressure were warning signs; the business account was the only proof that counted.

Good agents do not just "reply to messages". They move each request through the same steps every time, so nothing is missed and every customer gets the same quality. In Lesson 1.1 you saw the six stages. Now you will learn exactly what to do and say at each one.
A person organising several chat conversations
A repeatable workflow lets you handle many chats without losing track.
Step 1: Acknowledge quickly

The first reply tells the customer a human has seen them. It should come fast, even if you cannot solve the problem yet. Use their name, thank them and say what you are doing: "Hello Kemi, thank you for your message. I am checking your order now." A fast acknowledgement buys you time to do the real work properly.
Step 2: Clarify in one message
Many chats drag on because the agent asks one question at a time. Instead, ask for everything you need in a single, numbered message. Customers find numbered questions easy to answer on a phone.
Worked example: one clear clarifying message
For example, Ifeoma supports an online shoe store in Port Harcourt. A customer writes: "The shoes you sent are wrong."
Ifeoma acknowledges: "Hello Seyi, I am sorry about this. Let me fix it for you."
She sends one clarifying message: "To help quickly, please send: 1) your order number or the name used for the order, 2) a photo of the shoes you received, 3) the size and colour you ordered."
Seyi replies within 10 minutes with all three answers: order 2231, photo shows size 40, she ordered 41.
Ifeoma checks the order sheet: the order says 41. The warehouse packed the wrong size.
One message collected all the facts. Without it, Ifeoma would have needed three separate back-and-forth questions, and the customer would have waited longer.
Step 3: Check before you answer

Never guess. Check the order record, stock list, delivery notes or policy before replying. If you do not know, say "Let me confirm that for you" and find out. A wrong confident answer ("Your parcel arrives tomorrow") causes a second complaint when it does not.
Step 4: Solve or escalate

Decide whether you can solve the problem yourself. Each business should have simple rules about what agents can approve. For example, an agent might be allowed to arrange a free exchange for a wrong item, but need the owner's approval for any cash refund.

When you escalate, write a short summary so your supervisor does not need to read the whole chat: **who, what, what you have checked, what the customer wants, and the deadline**. Then tell the customer who is handling it and when they will hear back.
Step 5: Confirm with the customer

When the solution is in place, confirm it clearly and check it worked: "Your size 41 has been sent with our rider today. He will call you before delivery. Please return the size 40 to him. Is there anything else I can help with?" After delivery, a short check ("Did the new pair fit well?") shows care and tells you whether the case is truly solved.
Step 6: Log and close

Record the case in your tracking sheet with the date, channel, problem, action and outcome, and change the label to Resolved. You will build that sheet in Module 3. Logging only takes a minute but it is what lets you measure your work later.

Most support work is writing. Clear writing saves time because the customer understands the first time and does not need to ask again. Good support writing is **short, specific, warm and action-focused**.
A person writing an email on a laptop
A clear structure makes every reply easier to write and easier to read.
The structure of a good reply
**Greet and use their name:** "Hello Amina,"
**Acknowledge the request or feeling:** "Thank you for letting us know your order is late. I understand you needed it for Saturday."
**Give the answer or action:** "I have checked with our dispatch team. Your parcel is in Abuja and will be delivered tomorrow, Thursday, before 4 pm."
**State the next step:** "The rider will call you on 0803 xxx xxxx before arriving."
**Close warmly:** "Thank you for your patience. I am here if you need anything else."

Chat versus email

On WhatsApp or chat, keep messages to 2 to 4 short lines and send one idea per message if the topic is complex. Avoid sending ten tiny messages in a row; it floods the customer's phone. In email, use a clear subject, short paragraphs, and bullet points for steps or details. Email can be a little more formal: "Dear Mr Okafor" for a first formal complaint, "Hello Chidi" once you are in a friendly thread.

A single friendly emoji can soften a chat with a happy customer, but avoid emojis in complaints, refunds or formal emails. Match the customer's language where the business allows: if a customer writes in pidgin and your brand voice is relaxed, a light, respectful reply in the same style can build rapport. If unsure, use simple standard English.
Templates for common situations
Write templates once, test them, and save them as quick replies or email drafts. Here are four you will use often.
**Delay:** "Hello [name], I am sorry your order is taking longer than expected. It is currently [status]. The new delivery date is [day, time]. I will message you as soon as it leaves our office."

**Out of stock:** "Thank you for your interest, [name]. The [item] is out of stock right now. We expect new stock on [date]. I can reserve one for you, or suggest [alternative] which is available today."
**Need more information:** "To help you quickly, please send: 1) [detail], 2) [detail], 3) [detail]."

**Cannot do what they ask:** "I understand why you are asking for [request]. We are not able to [request] because [short honest reason]. What I can do is [option 1] or [option 2]. Which would you prefer?"
Worked example: rewriting a weak reply
For example, a customer asks a catering business in Lagos: "Can you do jollof for 80 guests on 14th?" The first draft reply was: "Yes we can do it, price depends, send details."
Problem 1: "price depends" gives no information. Fix: give a starting price per head and what changes it.
Problem 2: "send details" is vague. Fix: list the exact details needed.

Rewrite: "Hello Mrs Bello, thank you for thinking of us! Yes, we are available on the 14th. For 80 guests, jollof rice with chicken starts from about ₦3,500 per head, so roughly ₦280,000 (80 × ₦3,500), before delivery and serving staff."
Second message: "To give you an exact quote, please send: 1) venue area, 2) serving time, 3) whether you need servers and packs. I will send the quote within 2 hours of receiving these."
The rewritten reply answers the question, shows the calculation, lists exactly what is needed and gives a time for the quote. The customer can decide immediately.
Check templates before sending
The most common template mistake is sending one with a placeholder still in it, such as "Hello [name]" or the wrong price. Read every reply once before pressing send.

Every business gets complaints. A complaint handled well can turn an angry customer into a loyal one, because they see how the business behaves when things go wrong. A complaint handled badly can spread to the customer's friends and to public reviews. This lesson gives you a simple method and real scripts.
An angry face
Behind most angry messages is a real problem and a person who feels ignored.
Why customers get angry

Customers usually become angry when three things combine: something went wrong, they feel it was not their fault, and they think nobody is listening. You cannot always undo the first two, but you can fix the third immediately. That alone lowers the temperature.
The LAST method
A widely taught customer service approach is **LAST: Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank**. It was designed for face-to-face and phone service, but it works well in writing.

Listen
Read the whole message, including voice notes, before replying. Repeat the key facts back.
"So the cake arrived with the top damaged, two hours before your daughter's party. I understand how upsetting that is."
Apologise
Say sorry for the experience, sincerely and once. No excuses in the first line.
"I am truly sorry this happened on such an important day."
Solve
Offer a concrete fix or choices, with times.
"I can send a replacement cake by 4 pm, or refund the cake in full. Which would you prefer?"
Thank
Thank them for telling you and for their patience.
"Thank you for letting us know straight away. It helps us fix it."
LAST in a written complaint
Listen and restate facts
Apologise once, sincerely
Offer a fix or choices
Thank and follow up
Restating facts shows you listened; choices give the customer back some control.
Apologising without guessing fault

You can apologise for the customer's experience before you know whose fault it was. "I am sorry your parcel has not arrived" is honest. Avoid "It was our rider's fault" until you have checked; you might be wrong, and blaming a colleague or partner looks unprofessional. Once facts are confirmed, own the business's mistakes plainly: "We packed the wrong size. That was our error."
Language that calms and language that inflames
Calming: "I understand", "Let me fix this", "Here is what I can do", "You are right to expect better", "I will update you by 3 pm".
Inflaming: "Calm down", "As I said before", "That's our policy" (with no explanation), "You should have", silence for hours.
Avoid capital letters and many exclamation marks; in text they read as shouting.
Worked example: a full de-escalation chat

For example, Mariam supports a hair products shop in Ibadan. A customer, Tola, sends at 10:05 am: "THIS IS THE THIRD TIME I AM MESSAGING. I PAID ₦12,500 LAST WEEK AND NOTHING. YOU PEOPLE ARE SCAMMERS."

10:07 Listen and restate: "Hello Tola, I can see you paid ₦12,500 last week and have not received your order, and that you have had to message three times. I am sorry, that is not the service you should get."
10:08 Clarify: "Please send the name or phone number used for the order so I can find it immediately."
10:20 After checking: the order was packed but the address was missing a street name, so the rider could not deliver. Mariam does not blame the customer.

10:22 Solve with choices: "Your order is packed and ready. The rider could not find the address. Can you confirm your full address and a landmark? I can have it delivered today by 5 pm, or you can pick it up at our shop from 11 am."
10:25 Tola sends the address. 10:26 Thank: "Thank you, Tola. Delivery is booked for today before 5 pm. I will message you when the rider leaves."
2:40 pm: Mariam sends the rider's departure update. Next day: "Did everything arrive well?" Tola replies with a thank-you.
The customer went from accusing the business of fraud to thanking it within one day. Mariam also adds a step to her workflow: confirm full address and landmark at order time.
Public complaints and reviews

If a customer complains in a public comment or review, reply publicly once, briefly and politely, then move details to a private chat. Never argue in public or share order details there. Example: "Hello Tola, we are sorry about the delay with your order. We have sent you a message so we can fix this today." Other readers judge the business by this reply more than by the complaint.
When to stop and escalate

If a customer threatens harm, legal action, or a public campaign, or if the problem involves a product safety issue such as a skin reaction or food illness, escalate to your supervisor or the owner immediately and log it.

Policies, FAQs and escalation: keeping support honest and consistent
Write a clear FAQ and a short support policy for refunds, exchanges and delivery
Apply escalation rules consistently
Avoid dishonest support practices such as false promises and hiding problems
Handle product safety complaints responsibly

Customers trust a business that gives the same answer every time and keeps its word. That consistency comes from three written things: a **support policy**, a set of **FAQs**, and **escalation rules**. Without them, each agent makes up answers, and customers notice.
A person ticking off a checklist
Written policies mean every customer gets the same fair answer.
A one-page support policy
Ask the business owner to agree these points in writing. If you are the owner, decide them now. Keep the language simple enough to paste into a chat.
**Delivery:** areas covered, usual delivery times, who pays delivery, what happens if the customer is not available.
**Exchanges:** within how many days, condition of item (unused, with tags), who pays return delivery.
**Refunds:** when a refund is given, how (to the original payment account), who approves it, and how long processing takes.
**Damaged or wrong items:** what proof is needed (photo within a set time) and the remedy offered.
**Response times:** working hours and the first reply time customers can expect.
Consumer rights exist

Nigeria's Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018 protects consumers and is enforced by the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC). A business policy cannot simply remove a customer's basic rights. If you are unsure whether a policy is fair, the owner should seek proper advice.
FAQs: answer once, use many times

An FAQ (frequently asked questions) list collects the answers to the questions you get every day. Use your ticket sheet's Category column to find them: the categories with the most tickets are your FAQ topics. Put the FAQ on the website, in a WhatsApp catalogue description, or as a pinned post, and turn each answer into a quick reply.
Worked example: building FAQs from ticket data
For example, Funmi reviews her tracking sheet for one month: 120 tickets in total.
She counts tickets by category: Delivery time 42, Payment methods 25, Sizes 18, Wrong item 15, Product questions 12, Other 8.
Delivery time is 42 ÷ 120 = 0.35, so 35% of all tickets. Payment is 25 ÷ 120 ≈ 21%. Sizes are 18 ÷ 120 = 15%.
Those three categories together are 85 tickets, about 71% of the month's work.
She writes three FAQ answers (delivery areas and times, accepted payment methods, size guide with measurements) and adds them to the website and quick replies.
She also tells the owner that 15 wrong-item tickets suggest a packing check is needed.
Funmi now has evidence for where to focus. Clear FAQs should reduce repeated questions, and the next month's sheet will show whether they did.

A good FAQ answer is short, specific and complete. For example: "**How long does delivery take?** Within Lagos, 1 to 2 working days after payment is confirmed. Other states, 3 to 5 working days through our courier. Delivery fees depend on your area, and we confirm the fee before you pay." Review your FAQs every month against new ticket data. If a question keeps coming in even though it is in the FAQ, the answer may be unclear or hard to find, so rewrite it or move it somewhere more visible, such as the greeting message.
Escalation rules
Escalation levels for a complaint
Agent resolves within policy
Supervisor approves exceptions
Owner handles refunds, legal, safety
Each level has clear limits, so customers get fast answers and big decisions get the right approval.

Write down who handles what and how fast. For example: agent can approve exchanges within policy; supervisor approves anything outside policy within 1 working day; owner handles all refunds above an agreed amount, legal threats and safety issues the same day. The point is not bureaucracy: it is so the customer gets a quick, correct answer.
Honesty in support
**Do not promise what you cannot control.** Say "The courier estimates Thursday" rather than "It will definitely arrive Thursday".
**Do not hide known problems.** If a batch is delayed, tell waiting customers before they chase you.
**Do not fake reviews or pressure customers to delete complaints.** Fix the problem instead.
**Do not make up reasons.** "I will find out and update you by 2 pm" is always better than an invented answer.
Product safety complaints

If a customer reports harm (a skin reaction to a cosmetic, illness after food, an electric shock from a device), treat it as High priority. Express concern, advise them to stop using the product and to seek medical help if needed, ask for the product name, batch number and photos, and escalate to the owner immediately. Do not argue or say "Nobody else has complained". Regulated products such as food, drugs and cosmetics fall under NAFDAC in Nigeria, and the owner may need to act on the batch.
Do not give medical advice
As a support agent, you are not a health professional. Advise the customer to stop using the product and see a doctor or pharmacist if they have symptoms. Do not suggest treatments.

Metrics turn "I work hard" into evidence: "This week I handled 64 tickets, with an average first response time of 18 minutes and a resolution rate of 92%." Help-desk tools calculate these automatically, but you should understand exactly how, so you can calculate them from a simple sheet and explain them to an employer.
A bar chart
Numbers from your ticket sheet show what is working and what needs fixing.
The five core metrics
Metric
What it measures
Formula
First response time (FRT)
How long customers wait for the first human reply
First reply time minus time received; average = total of all FRTs ÷ number of tickets
Average resolution time
How long it takes to fully solve a case
Resolved time minus time received; average over resolved tickets
Resolution rate
Share of tickets solved in the period
Resolved tickets ÷ tickets received × 100
First contact resolution (FCR)
Share solved in the first reply, with no back-and-forth
Tickets solved in one reply ÷ resolved tickets × 100
Customer satisfaction (CSAT)
How happy customers were
Satisfied responses (for example 4 or 5 out of 5) ÷ all survey responses × 100

Automatic greeting and away messages do **not** count as a first response. FRT measures when a person actually replied. Many businesses measure FRT only within working hours, so a message at 11 pm counts from 8 am the next day; decide your rule and state it in your report.
Worked example: first response time
For example, Ada logs 5 WhatsApp tickets on Monday morning (working hours start 8:00 am).
Ticket 1: received 8:05, first reply 8:12 = 7 minutes.
Ticket 2: received 8:20, first reply 8:45 = 25 minutes.
Ticket 3: received 9:10, first reply 9:16 = 6 minutes.
Ticket 4: received 10:02, first reply 10:50 = 48 minutes.
Ticket 5: received 10:30, first reply 10:44 = 14 minutes.
Total = 7 + 25 + 6 + 48 + 14 = 100 minutes. Average FRT = 100 ÷ 5 = 20 minutes.
Average FRT is 20 minutes. Ticket 4 (48 minutes) pulled the average up; Ada notes she was in a meeting then, and plans to check chats between meetings.
Worked example: resolution rate, FCR and CSAT for a week

For example, Ada's weekly totals: 80 tickets received, 72 resolved by Friday, 45 of those solved in the first reply. She sent a 1 to 5 rating question to resolved customers and got 40 responses: 22 gave 5, 12 gave 4, 4 gave 3, 2 gave 1.
Resolution rate = 72 ÷ 80 × 100 = 90%.
Response rate to the survey = 40 ÷ 72 × 100 ≈ 56%, which she reports so readers know how many customers answered.
Ada's week: 90% resolution rate, 62.5% first contact resolution, 85% CSAT. The 8 unresolved tickets carry over to next week and must be listed.
Formulas in Google Sheets or Excel

If column B holds received time and column G holds first reply time (as full date and time), put **=(G2-B2)*24*60** in a new column to get minutes, because spreadsheets store time as fractions of a day. Then use **=AVERAGE(K2:K81)** for the average FRT. Count resolved tickets with **=COUNTIF(H2:H81,"Resolved")** and divide by **=COUNTA(A2:A81)** for the resolution rate.

Avoiding recruitment scams

Job scams target people looking for remote work. Why this matters
Your words are the whole experience

Online customer support means helping customers in writing, through a screen. The customer cannot see your smile. Everything she feels comes from three things.
Speed. A quick first reply, even if it only says you are checking.
Clarity. Short sentences, specific facts and a clear next step.
Follow-through. If you say, I will update you by 2 pm, you update her by 2 pm, even if the news is still waiting. Breaking a promise does more damage than a slow first reply.

Here is a simple rule. Keep quick things quick, and move serious things to a record. A customer who asks the price of a bag on WhatsApp should get the answer on WhatsApp.
A customer who wants a refund should still get a fast, warm reply, but the refund details should be confirmed in writing where the business can find them again, by email or in your tracking sheet.
And never promise money you are not allowed to approve.

Scan all new messages first, then prioritise.
Understand and check the record
Confirm with the customer
Every request, on any channel, moves through six stages. A message arrives, and you acknowledge it quickly.
You understand what she needs and check the record before you answer.
You solve it, or pass it to the right person.
You confirm with the customer, then log and close the case.

For example, Ngozi opens 7 new messages at 9 am. She scans all 7 first instead of answering the top one. Price questions get saved replies. A cracked jar gets an apology and an update promised by 2 pm. All 7 had a first reply within 30 minutes.

Three scams to spot
A screenshot and a rush to release goods. Confirm the money is in the business account first.
I sent too much, please refund the difference. Check the real balance and get owner approval.

Scammers target both customers and businesses. First, the fake payment alert. A customer sends a screenshot and asks you to release goods quickly. Screenshots prove nothing. Confirm the money has landed in the business account.
Second, overpayment. I sent 50,000 instead of 5,000 by mistake, please refund 45,000. Check the real balance first, and refund only with the owner's approval.
Third, asking for codes. A real business never needs a customer's PIN, OTP, password or WhatsApp code. Turn on two-step verification for the business number.

Why this matters

Good agents do not just reply to messages. They move each request through the same steps every time, so nothing is missed.
Most support work is writing. Clear writing saves time, because the customer understands the first time.
And a complaint handled well can turn an angry customer into a loyal one.
Step by step
The six-step support workflow
Give a time, not just a promise: by 3 pm today, not soon.
Acknowledge quickly, with her name
Clarify: all questions in one numbered message
Check the record before you answer
Solve, or escalate with a short summary
Confirm the fix and check it worked
Log the case and label it Resolved
Step one, acknowledge quickly. Hello Kemi, thank you for your message. I am checking your order now.
Step two, clarify in one message. Ifeoma asked: please send 1, your order number, 2, a photo of the shoes, 3, the size and colour you ordered. One message collected all the facts.
Step three, check before you answer. Never guess. A wrong confident answer causes a second complaint.
Step four, solve it, or escalate. Refunds, threats and suspected fraud go to your supervisor, with a short summary: who, what, what you checked, what she wants, and the deadline.
Step five, confirm the fix, and later check it worked. Did the new pair fit well?
Step six, log the case and change the label to Resolved.
I will get back to you soon means nothing. Say a real time, and set a phone reminder for every time you promise.
Writing
Greet and use her name
Acknowledge the request or feeling
Give the answer or action
State the next step and time
Close warmly
Every reply has five parts. Greet her by name. Hello Amina.
Acknowledge. I understand you needed it for Saturday.
Give the answer, near the top, because customers on phones may not read to the end. Your parcel is in Abuja and will be delivered tomorrow before 4 pm.
State the next step. The rider will call you before arriving.
Close warmly. On chat, keep it to 2 to 4 short lines. And read every template once before sending, so you never send Hello, name in brackets.

Warm, calm, professional
You did not read the policy
That is not our problem
We can't deliver on Sunday
ASAP
I am sorry this was not clear
Let me see what I can do
Would Monday morning work?
by 2 pm today
Some words push customers away. Blame, a flat no, and vague times like as soon as possible.
Replace blame with explanation. Replace can't with what you can do. And replace vague words with real times.

For example, a catering business in Lagos is asked about jollof for 80 guests on the 14th.
Naira prices are approximate.
Jollof with chicken, per head

The rewrite gives a starting price: from about 3,500 naira per head.

High priority means money taken but no goods, any safety issue, or a customer who has already chased twice. For example, Ruth logs a customer who paid 23,000 naira two days ago with no delivery. She chases dispatch at once.
Normal priority covers a wrong item, a late delivery within a reasonable time, and most complaints.
Low priority covers general questions and feedback. Answer them, but after the urgent cases.
Safety first
When a customer reports harm
You are not a health professional. Do not suggest treatments.
Treat it as High priority
Express concern; do not argue
Advise: stop using it, seek medical help
Ask for product name, batch number, photos
Escalate to the owner immediately
If a customer reports a skin reaction, illness after food, or a shock from a device, treat it as High priority.
Express concern. Never say, nobody else has complained.
Advise her to stop using the product and to see a doctor or pharmacist if she has symptoms.
Ask for the product name, batch number and photos.
Escalate to the owner immediately. Food, drugs and cosmetics fall under NAFDAC, and the owner may need to act on the batch.
Remember, you give no medical advice and suggest no treatments.

Hiding a known delay
Pressure to delete complaints
An invented reason
Honest
The courier estimates Thursday
Tell waiting customers first
Fix the problem instead
I will update you by 2 pm
Customers trust a business that keeps its word. So do not promise what you cannot control, do not hide known problems, and never make up a reason.
Say the courier estimates Thursday. Tell waiting customers about a delay before they chase you. And when you do not know, say: I will find out and update you by 2 pm.

First response time, worked out
Automatic greeting and away messages do not count.
For each ticket: first reply minus time received
Add all the waiting times

First response time is how long customers wait for the first human reply. Ada logs 5 tickets. The waits are 7, 25, 6, 48 and 14 minutes.
Added together, that is 100 minutes.
Divide by 5 tickets, and her average is 20 minutes.
An average can hide problems. One ticket waited 48 minutes, while Ada was in a meeting. So she plans to check chats between meetings.

45 solved in the first reply, out of 72 resolved.

Resolution rate is resolved tickets divided by tickets received, times 100. Ada resolved 72 of 80, so 90%.
First contact resolution is the share solved in the first reply. 45 of 72 gives 62.5%.
CSAT, customer satisfaction, is happy ratings divided by all responses. 34 of 40 gave 4 or 5, so 85%. Always say how many customers answered.
And never close tickets too quickly just to raise a number. That lowers satisfaction.

Three cases that show your range
A routine request handled efficiently
A problem solved through the workflow
A challenging case: anger, refund or scam
Pick three interactions that show different skills. First, a routine request, like a pre-sale question answered with a personalised quick reply.
Second, a problem solved through the workflow, like a wrong item: your clarifying message, the check, the fix and the confirmation.
Third, a challenging case. An angry customer, a refund outside policy, or a suspected scam.
Not working in support yet? Role-play realistic cases with a friend, and label them clearly as practice. Never present a practice case as a real job.

Your replies, in order, with times

Grace practised a case: a customer whose phone charger did not work, and who was embarrassed because it was a gift. Context: WhatsApp, 11:02 am.
Her replies: an apology at 11:04, one numbered clarifying message at 11:05, and an offer of a replacement or refund at 11:20.
Her reasoning: I offered two choices because the customer felt embarrassed and needed some control back.
Outcome: replacement delivered at 3:40 pm, rating 5 out of 5.
Reflection: I suggested adding a test before dispatch step.
Before sharing, replace names with Customer A, remove phone numbers, addresses and order numbers, and blur screenshots, including the profile photo.
Job safety
Real job or likely scam?
Remote support jobs are real, with titles like chat support agent or virtual assistant. A genuine offer has a clear company name, an interview first, and pay agreed in writing.
Stop and check if you are asked for a registration, training or equipment fee, if pay is far above normal, or if there is no interview. A genuine employer pays you. You do not pay them to work.
Never share your BVN, card PIN, OTP or passwords during recruitment.
Interviews
Answer with STAR
Situation: what was happening
Task: what you needed to do
Action: exactly what you did
Result: what happened, what you improved
Zainab is asked: tell me about a time you dealt with an angry customer. Situation: a customer wrote in capitals that we were scammers, after paying 12,500 naira and waiting a week.
Task: I needed to calm her, find the order and get it delivered.
Action: I restated her problem, apologised, asked for her order name in one message, and found the address had no street name.
Result: it was delivered that afternoon, and I added a landmark question to our order form.

Your 90-day plan
Targets from your own baseline
Record your baseline metrics
Choose one system and one skill
Set 2 or 3 dated targets
Link each target to an action
Review every 2 weeks, same rules
A baseline is where you are now. Uche's average first response time was 45 minutes, and her resolution rate was 82%.
Set two or three targets with dates. Uche aims for under 30 minutes by day 60, and 90% resolution by day 90.
Link each target to an action. She will check chats every 30 minutes, and review Waiting for us at 5 pm daily. A target without an action is only a wish.
Review every 2 weeks with the same rules. And keep your working hours. Faster replies should come from better habits, not from answering chats at midnight.
